The @IEA has once again revised historical annual data for oil consumption (it does so every August), resulting in some significant upgrades to global demand. 

The net result is that 20025 oil consumption is now estimated at 104.8m b/d (that's ~300,000 b/d higher than the last estimate, and ***a huge 1.1m b/d higher*** than where the IEA pegged a year ago 2025 demand). 

Despite the huge revision to demand forecasts, the IEA still sees the market last year as oversupplied, with supply running at 106.3m b/d on average. 

The changes also mean that the 105.7m b/d of oil consumption that the IEA now anticipates for 2027 is **higher** than the absolute peak oil demand it forecast a year ago (when it said that global oil consumption would peak in 2029 at 105.6m b/d).

CHART OF THE DAY: @IEA estimates Chinese EV fleet (cars + trucks) is displacing >1.5m b/d of oil demand (up from ~1m b/d) a year ago.

"This displacement [...] suggests an acceleration in the already very strong growth in the use of electricity for transportation," the IEA said. https://t.co/pI5JvTE0uG

CHINA’s production of electric and other new energy vehicles has more than doubled in the last three years. Production accelerated to 1.6 million units in June 2026 up from 1.2 million a year ago and just 0.7 million in June 2023. The deployment of new energy vehicles on massive scale is rapidly changing the composition of the vehicle fleet. New energy vehicles are on course to make up roughly one quarter of all registered cars by the end of the decade:

Strait of Hormuz over the last 24 hours: Iran learns the Twitter game

The US has dominated the Iran war so far in one category: the jawbone.

Iranian diplomats like Araghchi and Ghalibaf are either too stupid, too naive, or complicit to realize that the US is absolutely kicking Iran's ass in the media game.

We've had countless ceasefire announcements, the Strait of Hormuz is opening soon, and a peace deal is coming headlines over the last 5 months. Oil traders have already experienced VAR (value-at-risk) shocks, so taking outright long positions isn't possible for many large trading firms.

But it seems the Iranians are learning the Twitter game with hardliners now taking firmer control over both the public communication channels and the diplomacy routes.

Soon after another bogus headline from Pakistan about how the US and Iran are going to reach some permanent peace deal soon, the newly appointed Mohsen Rezaee denied all of it with his posts about the conditions the US needs to meet.

I suspect oil market participants are taking notice as well as oil prices completely disregarded the Pakistani headline, Chris Wright's bogus claim about ~9 million b/d moving through the Strait, and Trump's comments. 

Either way, we will see soon enough what the next escalation roadmap looks like. It won't be long.

Global observed oil inventories plunged by 69 mb in July, as renewed disruptions to exports from the Gulf and the Black Sea resulted in sharply lower volumes of oil on water. Onshore stocks declined by a modest 6 mb, as the pace of IEA emergency stock releases slowed, and despite continued draws in Chinese crude oil stocks. Refineries are enjoying exceptionally strong margins amid tightness across refined products, particularly middle distillates such as diesel, jet fuel and heating oil. The squeeze reflects the loss of supply from two critical refining regions: the Middle East, where disrupted crude flows and refinery outages have curtailed exports, and Russia, where Ukrainian attacks continue to constrain refinery runs.

The Middle East matters disproportionately to the distillate market. Before the war, the region accounted for more than 10% of global refining capacity and had developed into a major export-oriented refining hub, supplying 3.3 million barrels per day of refined products in 2025. Gulf refineries also benefit from ready access to medium and heavier sour crude grades that are particularly well suited to complex refineries configured to maximise yields of diesel, jet fuel and other middle distillates.

The loss of these barrels is therefore difficult to replace quickly, especially with Russian refinery runs also curtailed. The IEA has highlighted diesel and jet fuel as particularly vulnerable to an extended loss of Middle Eastern production and exports, given limited spare flexibility elsewhere in the global refining system.

As the charts highlight, the result has been a surge in distillate cracks well above gasoline margins across the US, Europe and Asia, while the NYMEX 3-2-1 crack spread has climbed to exceptionally elevated levels. In short, refiners able to secure crude and maintain high utilisation rates are currently being handsomely rewarded for a global shortage of refining capacity in precisely the part of the barrel the market needs most.

Some of the world's largest refiners include Sinopec, Saudi Aramco, ExxonMobil, Marathon Petroleum and Valero. The latter two, with their significant exposure to the US refining market, have seen their share prices more than double year to date, highlighting the extraordinary improvement in refining economics as global product shortages have driven crack spreads sharply higher.
